chapter_theme: The sage's lesson on austerity continues: the vows and their fruit, the seven doors of merit, compassion and equanimity, knowledge as a lamp, the four kinds of meditation, and the great ones who conquered their deeds, down to the lands of enjoyment won by givers.

cast.role: the austere sage who teaches King Payapati
King Payapati, who is taught and who is told his own line conquers karma

2001.reading: The sage says that the vows, though many and widely spread, are gathered into five, and that to tell their fruit across the heads that follow would leave the fitting vow short of its due.
2001.nuance: The count and the closing comparison (line 4) turn on the compressed phrase in lines 2 to 3 and cannot be fixed with confidence.

claims.claim: the many vows are gathered into five heads

2002.reading: All vows are alike in kind, the sage says, yet for those who are like the vowless the vow of not killing is the one that, if kings keep it, leaves nothing they cannot conquer.
2002.nuance: Winning (வெல்லா வகையில்லை) is put in the language of a king's conquest, so non-killing is offered to a ruler as a form of victory, not as a surrender of power. Lines 1 to 2 are hard to construe.

claims.claim: the vow of not killing, kept by kings, leaves no conquest beyond them

2003.reading: The austerity borne by those who possess themselves is hard even for the sages to tell if asked, the sage says; it belongs to those who have left this life with the zeal that shines in the next world.
2003.nuance: The sage answers the king's search for a refuge at his feet (1862) by saying first that what he asks is hard to put into words.

claims.claim: true austerity belongs to those who have left this life for the next with zeal

2004.reading: Those who came having done austerity stand firm in it, but for those who came having done wrong it is greatly hard, and the sage asks what can be done for people who suffer from the deeds they have done.
2004.nuance: Lines 3 to 4 may be the king's question to the sage; the sage is taken as the speaker because 2005 answers directly in his voice.

claims.claim: those who have done wrong find the state of austerity hard to reach

2005.reading: The wealth of austerity that the clear-sighted take up grows in two kinds and many, so do not be bewildered when it comes, but understand it fully.
2005.nuance: The king's own talk of sowing more seed (1842) is answered here: austerity is called wealth, and wealth that increases.

claims.claim: the wealth gained by austerity grows in kinds and multiplies

2006.reading: The sage says that if one strives to give worship without measure to the great lord of the three worlds, the gods themselves come to hail one as their chief.
2006.nuance: கலகையில் in line 2 may be a damaged spelling of 'countless' (அளவற்ற); the sense follows that guess.

claims.claim: worship of the lord of the three worlds makes one the chief of the gods

2007.reading: The sage says that the doors of merit that he has praised gather into four, yet those who have looked closely along the subtle texts count still more doors.
2007.nuance: Four is named here and seven in the next verse; the sage offers his four as a summary and defers to the finer count of the texts, so the two numbers are not a contradiction.

claims.claim: merit enters by doors that the texts count in different numbers

2008.reading: The seven doors are named: compassion, clarity, love for virtues, praise that reaches the object, faultless austerity, pure knowledge, and meditation that clears the dark.
2008.nuance: Compassion heads the list and meditation closes it, so the order runs from feeling to inner discipline.

claims.claim: merit has seven doors: compassion, clarity, love of virtue, praise, austerity, knowledge and meditation

2009.reading: When a dear life suffers, one should melt as for one's own life and save it; where that cannot be done, a moist heart is still the nature of compassion.
2009.nuance: Line 3 allows that rescue may not succeed and still counts inward tenderness as compassion, which makes the heart's state, not the result, the measure.

claims.claim: compassion is to feel another's suffering as one's own and to keep a moist heart even where relief fails

2010.reading: Whether abused, praised or left alone, those of clear mind feel no hot anger, no cool delight and no dislike, and are free of the three kinds of delusion.
2010.nuance: The three delusions (மும்மூடம்) are not named in the verse; the reading stays with what the Tamil says.

claims.claim: the clear-minded stay level to abuse, praise and neglect and are free of three delusions

2011.reading: The sage names love of the feet of the knowing, honouring the conduct of the great and looking to their many virtues as attachments that bring wealth when they do not bind.
2011.nuance: The line 'செறிதலி லார்வங்கள்' (attachments without binding) is the key phrase and is not fully secure.

claims.claim: love directed to the worthy brings wealth

2012.reading: Taking up austerity by one's strength, practising it, mastering it, standing first in conduct and praising it: this, the sage says, is the course that carries to the two heavens.
2012.nuance: The verse names the two heavens (இருவிசும்பு) without saying which they are.

claims.claim: austerity taken up by strength and practised leads to the two heavens

2013.reading: Those who have cut off their astringent stain and reached the rare state, standing first in this conduct, are what the sage calls good austerity, and it brings rule of the heavenly world.
2013.nuance: துவர்ப்பு, the astringent taste or dye, is read here as the stain of passion that the renouncer has shed; this reading is not certain.

claims.claim: conduct held first by those who have cut off passion is good austerity and brings rule of heaven

2014.reading: Knowledge is what the learned grasp on hearing the meaning of the texts: it clears the confusing darkness and is the lamp that shows the truth.
2014.nuance: Knowledge is a lamp, and the same lamp is lit in 2018 for vision, so the sage joins hearing and seeing.

claims.claim: knowledge gained by hearing the texts dispels delusion and shows the truth

2015.reading: The sage says that the meditation which grows on and on, fully told, is of four kinds, of which two bring the opposite of good and the rest give victory, heaven and release.
2015.nuance: The four are not named in the verse; the reading rests on the count and the two fruits.

claims.claim: meditation is of four kinds, two leading to ill and two to heaven and release

2016.reading: Those who strive in praise of merit find these things within, the sage says, and if one takes up the reverse of them it is a ripening that wears one down and torments.
2016.nuance: The first line is obscure; it probably speaks of the two bad meditations of 2015.

claims.claim: the opposite of the merit-bearing practice ripens into torment

2017.reading: Those worthy who have lit the lamp named vision, though without vows, rule not a dark realm but the world of the gods, or plunge into the flood of great bliss from which there is no return.
2017.nuance: The verse sets vision above vows without dismissing vows, and it leaves open which of the two destinations is meant.

claims.claim: right vision lit without vows still leads to heaven or to bliss without return

2018.reading: The sage says that seeing the true thing is the lamp of vision, and if it is lit the fire-darkness called deeds cannot stay, so he urges the king to make it his own wealth.
2018.nuance: Karma is called both fire and darkness, the lamp ending it by showing the true thing and by no act of a god.

claims.claim: the lamp of right vision destroys the darkness of karma
right vision should be held as one's own wealth

2019.reading: If one traces the gods and men in order, the sage says, Vijayan and the discus-lord are the first of eighteen who will come to bewilder this world.
2019.nuance: The eighteen and the identity of the discus-lord (Tivittan) turn on a compressed line and a rare form, so this reading is uncertain.

2020.reading: The sage says he has told of Ayakanthan who lost the discus and of the nine foes of the strong lord who fell, and that such falls are without end through the ages of the wide world.
2020.nuance: The names are as printed; line 2 is hard to parse and the count of foes is read from மும்மூவர்.

2021.reading: Among the gods and men who conquer their deeds, the sage says, the king himself is one, and with him Bharata, the first of his line, and the discus-rulers are those very ones.
2021.nuance: The king is told that his own line belongs to those who conquer karma, so renunciation is shown as a family inheritance and not an alien road.

claims.claim: gods and men who conquer their deeds include the king and his ancestor Bharata

2022.reading: Those with the sacred mark on the breast, who hold the glory of never being born again, are the best in this world, the sage says, and they come through austerity.
2022.nuance: The sacred mark on the breast (திருமறு மார்பர்) is taken as the Jain sign of a teacher of the path; other readings are possible.

claims.claim: those who win release from rebirth are the best in the world and come by austerity

2023.reading: The people who stand first in giving and like virtues, the sage says, are of this kind, having entered the grace of the gods and reached lands of enjoyment, though their nature cannot be fully told.
2023.nuance: The verse marks the lower rung of merit as enjoyment of lands, after 2022 has named release as the higher.

claims.claim: givers and the virtuous reach lands of enjoyment through their giving

links.note: 1862 has the minister name the austere sage's feet as the only refuge; 2003 is the sage's first reply, that austerity is hard to say even for sages.
links.teaches: The refuge sought in 1862 answers only by admitting that the thing sought is hard to put into words, so the king must be taught in steps.

links.note: 1842 has the king ask for more seed to sow for austerity; 2005 calls the harvest of austerity a wealth that grows in kinds.
links.teaches: The sage turns the king's idea of sowing into a promise that the austerity crop multiplies, so the vow rests on growth and not only loss.

links.note: 2002 offers the vow of not killing to kings as one that leaves no conquest out of reach; Kural 325 ranks not-killing highest among those who renounced.
links.teaches: The epic recasts non-killing as a king's way to win, where the couplet ranks it only among renouncers.

gains.a: The sage's claim for kings gains a ranking from the Kural, which sets non-killing above every other renunciation.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler as its audience: a king who keeps the vow and still seeks conquest, which it never considers.

links.note: 2009 defines compassion as melting for another's life and counts a moist heart where rescue fails; Kural 315 calls understanding useless without guarding another's pain as one's own.
links.teaches: The pairing shows compassion as both the test of understanding and a state that stays even when help fails.

gains.a: Compassion gains a test, since understanding is judged worthless without it.
gains.b: The couplet gains an allowance for failure: the moist heart still counts where the pain cannot be removed.

links.note: 2010 asks equal calm toward abuse, praise and neglect; Kural 151 asks the bearing of scorn only.
links.teaches: Level calm includes praise, so the couplet's forbearance covers only half of what the sage asks of the clear-minded.

gains.a: Equanimity gains the image of the earth that bears the digger, a reason to take scorn without answer.
gains.b: Forbearance gains the other side, praise, which also stirs the heart and needs the same steadiness.

links.note: 2014 makes hearing the meaning of the texts a lamp that clears delusion; Kural 423 makes wisdom seeing the true thing in whatever is heard.
links.teaches: The sage trusts the text as source, where the couplet makes the hearer's seeing the test of any source.

gains.a: Knowledge from hearing gains a check, seeing what is true in the words and not trusting the speaker.
gains.b: The couplet gains an end for its seeing: the clearing of the darkness that binds one to deeds.

links.note: 2014 calls knowledge from the texts a lamp; 2018 calls seeing the true thing a lamp of vision that ends the dark.
links.teaches: One lamp is lit twice, once by hearing and once by seeing, so the sage joins the two as stages of one light.

links.note: 2018 has the lamp of vision end the darkness of deeds; Naladiyar 51 has the lamp of austerity end sin as darkness dies, and darkness return when the oil runs out.
links.teaches: The lamp's light is credited to vision in the epic and to austerity in the quatrain, with only the quatrain saying the light can fail.

gains.a: The lamp of vision gains the warning of the oil, that light can go out unless fed.
gains.b: The quatrain's lamp gains a source in the knowing of the true thing, where it names only austerity.

links.note: 2018 has vision destroy karma's darkness by itself; Tirumanthiram 116 has Nandi remove the malas as fire rises from bamboo, out of grace.
links.teaches: Release by one's own seeing, without any god, meets release by a lord's grace, and the same fire-and-darkness language serves both.

gains.a: The lamp of vision gains a rival cause, grace, for the same burning away of the dark.
gains.b: The grace-fire gains the Jain demand that the soul's own seeing bear the work, so the cause is not left wholly with the lord.

links.note: 2015 sorts meditation into four kinds by their fruit, two bad and two leading to heaven and release; Tirumanthiram 598 gives three objects of meditation, Shakti, the Supreme and Siva as guru.
links.teaches: The two works sort meditation differently, by moral fruit in the epic and by the divine object in the Saiva text.

gains.a: The fourfold sorting gains named objects, since it never says what is to be fixed upon.
gains.b: The Saiva list gains a test of fruit, that some meditation leads astray as well as upward.

links.note: 2017 says those with the lamp of vision reach heaven or the bliss without return even without vows; Kural 356 says those who learn and see the true thing reach the path of no return.
links.teaches: The epic loosens the couplet's chain, holding that sight alone, even without vows, opens heaven or release.

gains.a: The vowless seer gains a precedent, since the couplet already gives seeing the true thing the path of no return.
gains.b: The couplet gains the claim that vows are not required, which it never says, and the lesser reward of heaven.

source_issues: 2001, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2011 and 2016 turn on compressed or damaged lines and are marked uncertain.
The speaker of these verses is the sage by the story, not named in any of the lines; 2004 may be in the king's voice.
